one_liner: RocksDB fork whose workload-driven compaction and write-stall policy (Arce) beats RocksDB leveling when read/write mixes shift.
what_it_does: A research fork of RocksDB (default 'prod' branch built on RocksDB 9.5, on-disk 'dev' branch on 11.2) that drops fixed level capacities and run counts (ElasticLSM). The tree becomes a set of timestamp-ordered sorted runs, and a compaction may merge runs within one level, into the next level, or across several levels at once. You opt in through Options: on prod, compaction_style = kCompactionStyleDynamic plus a raw AdaptiveCompactionController*; on dev, kCompactionStyleArce plus a shared_ptr ArceCompactionController. Get/Put/iterators are unchanged RocksDB, but you must tell the controller the expected range/update/point mix yourself.
how_it_is_fast: Each candidate compaction gets an 'effectiveness score': M times its long-term benefit (runs removed x (range + FPR x point) lookup cost) minus a short-term penalty for the reads slowed and writes stalled while it runs. Only non-dominated candidates can win, meaning none removes more runs in less time. Write stalls are decoupled from level shape: in the prod code, writes slow once the count reaches a threshold c and stop at 4c. A background simulation over a windowed cost model (one window = memtable size / entry size updates) grid-searches (M, c) on 16 OpenMP threads and reruns when the average run count drifts more than 10%. In read-heavy phases this yields multi-level merges that cut runs faster than Leveling; in write-heavy phases it defers compaction more than Tiering.
when_to_use: Reproducing or extending workload-aware LSM compaction research (against Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL, LazyLeveling) on a RocksDB code base with ~1 KB values, as in the paper (24 B keys, 1000 B values).
Read/write mixes that shift over time (for example, write-heavy ingest followed by read-heavy serving), where you know or can measure the mix and pass it to the controller.

Write-heavy to balanced phases where leveled RocksDB is stall-bound. The prod README's tmpfs table shows the largest gains at 10-40% reads (2.87x to 1.39x lower total time), mostly on the write side: 183.7 s vs 702.7 s of write latency at 10% reads.
In-memory or tmpfs single-column-family stores with one compaction stream, which is the setup the prod branch was adapted to (a TikTok recommendation service) and the setup both repo harnesses test.
Linux x86-64 with GCC and OpenMP available; the paper and README results are from an i9-13900K on Ubuntu 22.04.
when_not_to_use: Production systems that need a supported RocksDB: 1 star, no releases, and the default branch says it is not a faithful implementation of the paper.

Steady read-dominated workloads. At 90% reads the prod gain is about 9% (438 s vs 479 s), and the paper shows ArceKV trailing 1-Leveling and Leveling right after an abrupt write-to-read shift (workload B to D).

On-disk stores sensitive to insert latency or SSD wear. The dev README's on-disk run has higher insert latency (2.45 us vs 2.15 us) and 54% more compaction writes (426 GB vs 276 GB) than leveled compaction.

Setups that rely on parallel compactions. Both branches assume one compaction decision stream: dev logs a warning when max_background_jobs or max_background_compactions is above 1 ('may lead to unstable run indexing'), and the paper's evaluation used one compaction thread.
Workloads that need range filters or an up-to-date upstream: prod removed the range-filter policy and is pinned to RocksDB 9.5.

integration.form: static lib (a full RocksDB source fork built with CMake; it replaces librocksdb instead of linking beside it)
integration.dependencies: prod: gflags, OpenMP (REQUIRED in CMakeLists; <omp.h> is included from a public header), and the grafite git submodule (SSH URL git@github.com:marcocosta97/grafite.git, pulling sux and sdsl-lite headers) included by table/block_based/filter_policy_internal.h. The tools/arce_bench harness also links TBB. dev: gflags, with OpenMP optional (WITH_OPENMP=ON by default, falls back to serial) and no submodules. RocksDB's usual optional compression libraries apply to both.
integration.min_toolchain: prod: C++17 (RocksDB 9.5 base), CMake 3.10+. dev: C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20, RocksDB 11.2 base). Compiler versions are not documented beyond 'gcc/g++'.
integration.platforms: Tested only on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, i9-13900K). Other RocksDB platforms are not documented, and prod will not build on a toolchain without OpenMP.
integration.thread_safety: Normal RocksDB DB-handle thread safety. Controller state is guarded by a std::mutex, but the compaction policy assumes one active compaction decision at a time (prod's picker bails out if a chosen file is already being compacted, and dev warns when background jobs are above 1).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same RocksDB API, but you build this fork instead of upstream, set a non-upstream compaction_style and controller object, and supply workload ratios yourself; compatibility of the resulting DB directories with upstream RocksDB is not documented

gotchas: prod: the AdaptiveCompactionController is a raw pointer in Options that the README example allocates with new and never frees. Its constructor spawns a detached thread that captures this and loops with 5 s sleeps, so deleting the controller while that thread is alive is a use-after-free. DB::Open also blocks in find_first_mc_when_ready(), polling once a second until the first tree state appears, and prints timings to stdout.

prod: ColumnFamilyData::RecalculateWriteStallConditions (db/column_family.cc) reads comp_controller->compactioner without a null check, so column families that do not use the dynamic style depend on the optimizer removing that dead load. The stall check also compares the L0 file count against c and 4c, while the simulation models total runs. The README's cmake line '-CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' is a typo; use -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, because RocksDB's CMakeLists makes a git checkout a Debug build by default.

dev: if arce_compaction_controller is null, PickCompaction builds a fresh default controller on every call, so the (M, c) grid search reruns on every pick with a default update-only workload. Even with a controller, the search runs inside PickCompaction (which RocksDB calls with the DB mutex held), and both branches call omp_set_num_threads(16), which changes the OpenMP thread count for the whole process.

The library does not measure the workload mix. You pass range/update/point proportions (prod: once, at construction; dev: via SetWorkloadProportions, which the dev harness calls at each phase change). The paper's online workload-statistics module and Eigen/SIMD score vectorization are not present in either branch.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ArceKV over Titan or DobLIX when the problem is compaction and write-stall policy under a read/write mix that changes over time with ~1 KB values: Titan targets large values through key-value separation, and DobLIX speeds up SST index lookups but gains only 1.04x on write-heavy loads. If you can leave RocksDB's format entirely and want bigger raw write gains from a maintained engine, pick SplinterDB, KVell or F2 instead.
verified_claims_summary: In PVLDB 19(5):958-972 (2026), on an i9-13900K with 128 GB RAM capped to 75 GiB, NVMe/ext4, one flush and one compaction thread, and two 245.76M-operation compound workloads, ArceKV's average throughput was 2.00x and 1.41x that of 1-Leveling (RocksDB's default style, reimplemented on the RocksDB-based Moose framework) and 2.17x-2.92x that of Tiering and LazyLeveling; no compiler or flags are stated, and the abstract's '~3x' is measured against the slowest baseline. The prod README's own test (tmpfs, one thread, point reads plus inserts, uniform keys, 64 MB memtable, no compression, compared against RocksDB 9.5 leveled compaction with dynamic level bytes off) shows 2.87x lower total time at 10% reads, shrinking to 1.09x at 90%.
status_note: An active research artifact (last push 2026-04-29, 1 star, 0 issues, no releases), dual-licensed GPLv2/Apache-2.0 like RocksDB; using it means building the whole fork, with prod as the in-memory TikTok adaptation and dev as the on-disk port on RocksDB 11.2.
